description_full: Lear Corporation designs, develops, engineers, manufactures, assembles, and supplies automotive seating, and electrical distribution systems and related components for automotive original equipment manufacturers in North America, Europe, Africa, Asia, and South America. Its Seating segment offers seat systems, keyseat components, seat trim covers, and seat mechanisms; and thermal comfort systems, such as seat heating, ventilation, active cooling, pneumatic lumbar and massage products, seat cushioning, and headrests, as well as surface materials, including leather and fabric for light trucks, compact cars, pick-up trucks, and sport utility vehicles. The company's E-Systems segment provides electrical distribution and connection systems that route electrical signals and networks; and manage electrical power within the vehicle for various powertrains. This segment's products comprise wire harnesses, terminals and connectors, engineered components, and junction boxes; electronic system products, including body domain control modules, and high voltage switching and power control systems. It also offers software and connected services, as well as cybersecurity software. The company offers its products and services under the GUILFORD, EAGLE OTTAWA, THAGORA, IGB AUTOMOTIVE, COMFORTFLEX BY LEARTM, LEAR, CONFIGURE+, FLEXAIR, INTU, RENEWKNIT, SOYFOAM, ProTec, and TeXstyle brands. The company was founded in 1917 and is headquartered in Southfield, Michigan.

financial_summary: Lear Corporation is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $5.3B market cap on $23.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 9% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, and 7% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $527M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.49× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.2× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 7.7×.

Management returns a meaningful 9.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.4× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.2x net debt to EBITDA ($1.0B of cash against $2.7B of debt), with interest covered 7.7x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.6% over 3 years, 6.4% over 5 years and 2.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 37% of profits supports about 3.4% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 20.1% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 2.4% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 8, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.

own: Insiders hold little stock (0.5%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (14 sales, net $10.0M sold).
It returns 9.2% a year to shareholders (6.1% in buybacks and 2.8% in dividends).

It has paid a dividend for 15 consecutive years, raising it 19.6% a year over the last five.
people: With about 164,300 employees, each generates about $142K of revenue, 0.4x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 3.6% a year.

CEO pay is $4.9M (35x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
